--- ASST 2026-09-23T16:13:01.263Z The report is written to [printer-setup-ux-review.md](printer-setup-ux-review.md) at the repo root, untracked and not committed. It comes from reading the code on `jusprin-newui` at 886098514b plus your four screenshots. I did not run the app.  **The root cause behind all five issues.** The printer chat is built as a three-phase state machine: identify, add, connect. Each phase has its own chrome, its own copy, and exactly one tool the model may call, and after the add the model gets no tools at all. The phase transitions happen outside the conversation. Adding a printer is a page chip, not a tool, and on success the C++ side pushes state but posts no message and starts no model turn. That is why screenshot 2 shows "Your printer has been added" above a thread whose last line is still the assistant refusing a 0.7 mm nozzle. The concrete code evidence is in section 3 of the report, with file and line references.  **Your five issues, traced.**  - The Home strip is the internal provenance enum leaking. The word "assumed" comes straight from `FactProvenance`. It was added when the panel lost its pinned card, and the receipt was moved to Home instead of into the thread. - The prepare-versus-connect explanation is hard-coded chrome, and the same distinction is also taught to the model in its prompt, so it explains it unprompted too. - The "added" panel is a separate region rendered above the message list. New content appears at the top while the thread stays stale. - "Go to Home" is a bare button with no class. Five more unstyled buttons sit in the same file, against the design-system rule. - The connection form has six states each mapped to a sentence. The model gets the state as JSON pasted into its system prompt, is told there are no tools, and never learns the outcome of an attempt unless the user types again.  **Other issues found, the worst first.** The assistant is deaf to every outcome, including connection success or failure. The boxed heading in screenshot 5 is a focus ring from a programmatic focus call. Chat lines run about 1,400 px wide in Add mode. The leave-confirmation dialog protects the developer's state, not anything the user values. Home nags every printer with "Not connected" and a full-width Connect button, including printers with no network. A nozzle mismatch sends the user to OrcaSlicer's settings dialog even though a change tool with a confirmation card already exists.  **The proposal.** The panel keeps only a back control, the thread, and the composer. Add and connect become mutation tools with approval cards in the thread, reusing the approval-card path that `printer_change` already uses. The connect card carries the single credential field, and the credential rides on the approval decision so it never enters the tool arguments, the result, or the thread. Every backend outcome posts a fact note and starts a turn, so the assistant writes the receipt and offers the next step. The prompt is rewri
--- ASST 2026-09-23T16:59:54.391Z Yes, I agree, and it goes further than you said: it removes almost every hard-coded button in the panel, not just those two.  **How it works**  The assistant ends a message with a short list of suggested answers. The app draws each one as a button under that message. Tapping a button does exactly one thing: it sends that text as the user's reply, the same as if the user had typed it. Nothing else is wired to the button. So "Keep 0.4 mm" and "Use 0.7 mm" are just two possible replies the assistant wrote down.  Because a tap is a reply, every confirmation becomes a normal exchange:  - "Is it the Anycubic Kobra 3?" with buttons "Yes, add it" and "No, a different one". The user taps "Yes, add it". The assistant then tells the app to save the printer, and says it is done. - "Which one is yours?" with a button per model name. - "I see a P1S named Workshop on your network. Connect to it?" with "Yes" and "Not now". - "You're all set." with "Done", which the assistant knows means close the panel.  The assistant asks the question, the user answers, then the assistant acts. That is the whole rule. No separate "Add this printer" row, no Keep/Set card, no Undo row, no "This one" and "Use this" buttons on cards. If the user wants to undo, they say "put it back to 0.4" and the assistant does it.  The one exception is a secret. An access code or API key must not pass through the assistant. So when the assistant needs one, the app shows a small card in the chat with one text field and a Connect button. The code goes straight from that field to the C++ connecting code. That is the only native input left, and it is about 40 lines.  **Layout**  The buttons sit directly under the assistant's message, in the same column as its text, left-aligned, as a row of pill-shaped chips that wraps onto more lines if needed. They look like the choices on a phone messaging app. Only the newest assistant message shows chips. When the user taps one, its text appears as the user's own bubble on the right, and the chips disappear. When the user starts typing instead, the chips fade, since a typed answer is always allowed. Chips are reachable by keyboard, Tab to move between them and Enter to choose.  Rough picture:  ``` ●  You have an Anycubic Kobra 3. I'll set it up with the 0.4 mm    nozzle it ships with. Is that right?     ( Yes, add it )  ( I changed the nozzle )  ( Different printer )                                                         Yes, add it  ▢  ●  Done. The Kobra 3 is ready. It looks like it runs Klipper, so    I can send files to it over Wi-Fi if you like.     ( Connect it )  ( Not now ) ```  **How the assistant sends the choices**  I recommend giving the assistant one small tool, call it "offer choices", that takes a list of short strings. The assistant writes its message, calls the tool as the last thing in its turn, and the app ends the turn there and attaches the strings to the message. Tool calls are reliable; a text conven
--- ASST 2026-09-23T17:09:01.327Z The handoff is written to [printer-setup-chat-handoff.md](printer-setup-chat-handoff.md) in the repo root, untracked and not committed, next to the review from earlier.  It is written for an agent that has not seen this conversation. It covers:  - **Context and the five decisions you made** so they are not reopened: assistant-chosen reply buttons, the hard-coded buttons folded into that mechanism, no memory across openings, full window everywhere, OrcaSlicer's wizard kept as the fallback. - **A map of the current code** with file paths and line numbers for everything that gets deleted or changed, plus the list of tests that encode the old design and must be rewritten. - **Target behaviour** as three worked conversations for Add, Change, and Connect, including the Bambu path. - **How reply buttons work.** I recommend the assistant end a message with a fixed line like `Choices: Yes, add it | Different printer`. The page strips that line and draws the chips. I traced why a tool would be worse: the chat host completes the message on every tool call and always starts a follow-up turn after the result, so a "show choices" tool would need new turn-ending logic in the core host. - **Nine tools**, all available for the whole session, with arguments and results. Add and change run immediately after the person's tapped or typed yes. Connect is the one tool with a card, because the access code must not pass through the assistant. The code travels from the card to C++ on the approve message, kept in a host-side map that never enters the tool record, and there is a required test that the code appears in no artefact. - **How a Bambu connection result reaches the assistant**: the panel's existing timer polls the backend once a second while an attempt is in flight, then posts a note and starts a turn. That replaces the page's polling loop. - **Constraints**: design tokens for the new chip, fork-stewardship rules, the CMake-built web bundles, absolute build paths, and the no-commit rule for working docs. - **Five ordered steps**, each with tests and a live verification using the fake Bambu printer, and the two lists of what the implementer decides alone versus asks you.

content.content:
## Tool budget and tool shape

Tool count is bounded by what a turn loads, not by what the app can do. The evidence behind these rules: OpenAI's function-calling guidance keeps fewer than 20 functions available at the start of a turn and defers the rest; Anthropic's [tool-writing guidance](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents) asks for a few tools targeting high-impact workflows and names "tools that merely wrap existing software functionality or API endpoints" as the common error; a [domain-oriented MCP study](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.22063v1) measured a generic thin-tool interface below raw SQL and domain-shaped tools far above both; and the "god tool" that dispatches many unrelated actions through one `action` parameter is a documented anti-pattern. The current five-tool MCP catalog measures about 1.9 KB per definition, two thirds of it output schema.

- **Loading, for now.** Every registered tool loads on every turn in both adapters: the in-app adapter sends the full function list with each request, and MCP `tools/list` returns the whole catalog. This is the simplest correct behaviour and it keeps the tools array byte-identical across a chat, which is what OpenAI's prompt cache keys on. The budget of 20 definitions per turn is a measured trigger, not a gate: the live regression records definition bytes, input tokens, and cached tokens per request, and the journey catalog below will exceed 20 definitions from its first milestone. That is accepted until those measurements show selection errors or context pressure.
- **The baseline, measured on Windows against the live app.** After M5: in-app 25 definitions and 29,148 bytes, MCP 26 and 33,013 over two `tools/list` pages. After M4: in-app 20 definitions and 21,594 bytes, MCP 21 and 24,923 (24,901 through the offline helper recipe). After M3: in-app 20 definitions and 19,331 bytes, MCP 21 and 22,661 (22,639 through the offline helper recipe). After M2: in-app 18 definitions and 12,721 bytes, MCP 16 and 13,911 (13,894 through the offline helper recipe). After M1: in-app 11 definitions and 6,482 bytes, MCP 9 and 6,915. At M0 it was in-app 7 and 3,145 bytes, MCP 5 and 3,147.

  The `--live-agent` regression at both points says what that costs. The first request of a conversation caches nothing and pays for the whole catalog: 803 tokens at M0, 1,733 at M1, so four more definitions cost about 930 tokens, once. Every later request in the same conversation came back 77 to 92 per cent cached (5,864 in, 5,376 cached at M1), because the tools array is byte-identical across a chat and that is what the cache keys on. At M2 the same regression's eleven requests took 2,875 to 6,763 input tokens with 42 to 91 per cent cached; none started cold, because an earlier run of the same day had warmed the cache for the shared prefix, so the M2 cold cost is not measured by that run.

  So the cost of a definition is what it adds to the *first* request of each conversation, not to every turn, and the budget stays a trigger rather than a gate. What would change that reading: a catalog large enough to make the first request of every conversation expensive on its own, or transcripts showing the model choosing the wrong tool. Watch both; neither has appeared yet.

- **It reads or changes OrcaSlicer state:** presets, the model, plates, slicing, the device list. The page never owns project state (see the constraints below).
- **It is a limit or a boundary the app must guarantee:** what a tool accepts and refuses, which tools a session may call, what needs the person's approval, and what reaches the model provider (API keys, access codes, project data). Page code can state a limit; only the app can enforce it.
- **It has to work without a page:** the MCP server, background work, tests that run without a browser.
- **It depends on a thread or a lifetime the page does not have.**

The printer panel is the example. The app sends the page facts only: sizes, spools, which printer is on a card, what a change changed. The page writes every word from them. It writes the model's instructions (`AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts`) and hands them over with `printer_instructions`. It writes the panel's own words, the opening line and the note that goes with each tap (`AgentUI/src/printerWords.ts`). The opening goes over with `printer_opening`, and a tap's note travels in the tap's payload.

The app decides which one tool each mode offers, checks every call, and refuses a turn that has no instructions rather than falling back to the project assistant's prompt. It posts the opening once per session, and a tap's note only when the tap goes through, bounded to 2 KB. It still writes the notes for what only it can find out when the tap arrives: the network printer has gone, its model id is not on the list, or a save or undo failed.

Windows uses WebView2, macOS uses WKWebView, and Linux uses WebKitGTK. Local resource packaging must work on all three. The demonstrated prototype used a single-file local bundle to avoid WKWebView `file:` subresource failures; production keeps that approach, and CMake now produces the bundle from the TypeScript/React sources.

content.text:
The guide's "one tool per mode" statement is stale. It was a deliberate design for a panel that no longer exists: the design was reversed on purpose on 2026-09-23, the guide was never updated, and nothing today says the old constraint should come back. There is one live pressure in its direction, described under "What's left of the old intent".

## Timeline

| Date | Commit | What `session_tools()` offered |
|---|---|---|
| 09-17 | `0e55c4f9be` | All four tools of that time (`printer_catalog_search`, `printer_propose`, `printer_suggest`, `printer_change`) in every mode. |
| 09-18 | `7f66e75b07` | One tool per mode: Add got `printer_identify`, Change got `printer_change`. This commit added the guide lines at ~95, ~289 and the two table rows. |
| 09-22 | `67577ad993` | Connect mode got no tools at all. |
| 09-22 | `4d4f9e466b` | "Replace printer summary card…": the pinned card was removed from the page. |
| 09-23 | `8334b3395b` | All eight tools in every mode. The code comment and the per-mode test were replaced by "every session offers every printer tool…". The guide was not touched. |
| 09-27 | `492fdb5531` | Edited the guide's `printer_change` table row but left "Change mode only". |

`bd81401da2` and `dae85d7970` (both 09-18) and `a9ec0277f5` (09-27) also edited the guide and left the one-per-mode text as it was.

## Why one tool per mode (`7f66e75b07`)

- **Commit message:** "the model decides and one tool per mode checks and carries out". The problem it was fixing was the app ordering the model around, plus a keyword search that misidentified printers. It gives no separate argument for restricting the tools.
- **Code comment and guide:** "A Change session that could identify a printer could also clear the card of the printer it is about."
- **What "the card" meant:** the pinned facts header (Printer, Nozzle, Plate, Filament). At `7f66e75b07`, `identify()` called `clear_proposal()`, which wiped those facts, so an identify call in Change mode would have blanked the header for the saved printer.
- **Is that reason still valid?** No. The pinned card was dropped from the page on 09-22 and its last C++ traces were deleted in `8334b3395b`. Today `identify()` only appends a picture-card block and clears nothing.
- **Other supporting text:** the guide's cache and size measurements for one definition per session. That is evidence about cost, not a reason for the rule.
- **Other docs:** `product-definition.md` has nothing on this. `architecture.md:137` says "The app decides which one tool each mode offers", which is equally stale.

## Why all tools in every mode (`8334b3395b` and its sessions)

- **Commit message:** "one assistant tool per phase" is listed among the problems of the old three-phase flow. The new panel is "only a conversation: the assistant adds, changes and connects printers through eight tools".
- **Where it came from:** the untracked handoff doc `printer-setup-chat-handoff.md`, recorded in Entire checkpoint `01M385D8DNVF1S28Q960NWJVH5`. Its design came from session `5f00eae1-…` (checkpoint session index 2); session `54c192d0-…` (index 1) implemented it.
  - Its diagnosis: the panel had "a different single tool for the assistant in each phase. The assistant is not told when phases change." Also, `profile()` "removes all tools once a printer is added".
  - Its prescription: "Every one of them is available for the whole session: `profile().tool_names` lists all of them, always." It also says to delete "`ConversationMode` gating of tools (keep the mode only to choose the opening line and which printer the session is about)".
  - The earlier UX-review reply in that session describes the same root cause: "exactly one tool the model may call, and after the add the model gets no tools at all."
  - Kenneth's own prompts that day ask for the assistant to guide the whole process instead of phase-by-phase UI. He never discussed tool gating directly.
- **Stated need for crossing modes:**
  - Add needs the connect tools: the worked Add example goes identify → add → "Connect it" → connect → finish in one conversation.
  - Connect is described as "the same as the Add conversation from 'Connect it' onward".
  - "Put it back to 0.4" is handled by the same change tool.
  - Nothing anywhere says Change or Connect needs `printer_identify` or `printer_add`. No-one argued it; it followed from "all tools, always".
- **Entire search:** `entire search` fails with "no matching repositories found for [TheSpaghettiDetective/JusPrin]", and `--all-repos` returns 0 hits. The findings above come from grepping the transcripts stored locally under `refs/entire/checkpoints/*`. Later checkpoints that mention the phrase (`01M3GKE71E…`, `01M3HGGA28…`, `01M3JCF2Z2…`) only quote the guide or code. None revisits the decision.

## What the code enforces per mode today (`PrinterConversation.cpp`)

**Mode checks.** Nothing in `preflight_tool`, `execute_tool` or the registry checks `m_mode`. Mode only sets the opening, which printer the session is about, whether the catalog and network are in `context`, and whether a Bambu session opens on the plug-in notice. Guards are keyed to whether a saved printer exists:

- **Connect tools:** `preflight_tool` covers only `printer_connect`. It returns `no_printer` when `m_printer_name` isn't saved, then does device/address checks. `connection_status` and `printer_manual_connection` return the same `no_printer` refusal. In practice these fail in an Add session until something has been added.
- **`printer_add` in a Change or Connect session:** not refused. It saves a new printer and sets `m_printer_name` to it, so the session is now about the new printer. The mode stays Change or Connect.
  - The only refusal is `already_added`, for the same catalog id twice in one conversation.
  - `printer_manual_setup` behaves the same way when the wizard adds printers.
- **`printer_change`:** takes a `printerName` and changes any saved printer, not only the one the session is about. That also works in Add mode before anything is added. The guide's table row ("the one saved printer the panel is about… Change mode only", "checked before its card… Undo reverses it") is wrong on all counts: there is no card and no Undo now.
- **`printer_identify` in Change or Connect:** harmless. It adds a picture block.
- **`printer_setup_finish`:** closes the panel in every mode.
- **Tests that pin today's behaviour:**
  - `tests/agent/test_printer_conversation.cpp:297` "every session offers every printer tool…"
  - `test_printer_conversation.cpp:1781` "the model is offered every printer tool…"
  - `tests/agent/test_openai_responses_agent.cpp:157`

## What's left of the old intent

The uncommitted work in this worktree steers per mode through the prompt, not the tool list. `printerInstructions.ts` sends the finding/adding rules "only while adding one, so a conversation about a printer the person already has is not steered toward adding it". A new `shell_harness` check asserts that a Change-session question ("what's the current start g-code?") calls neither `printer_add` nor `printer_identify`. It was added because the reply "once offered to add it first" (2026-09-28).

That is the only evidence I found of add tools causing trouble outside Add. The guide's own principles name "transcripts showing the model choosing the wrong tool" as the thing that would change its "every tool loads" reading. Whether this bug counts as that is unclear: the transcript shows an offer to add, not a wrong call.

## Relevant general principles in the guide (~86–95)

- "Every registered tool loads on every turn", which keeps the tools array byte-identical and cacheable.
- The 20-definition budget is "a measured trigger, not a gate".
- A tool-set switcher that rewrites the tools array breaks the cache and "is not to be built".

Eight fixed tools per session fits these principles. The line-95 bullet presents the panel as "the exception to 'every tool loads'", which is no longer true.

## Stale text to fix

- `agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md:95` — the one-per-mode claim, the "clear the card" reason, and the one-definition measurements.
- `mcp-tool-extension-guide.md:289` — "offers one of them per mode", "two tools".
- `mcp-tool-extension-guide.md:354-355` — the table rows. Six of the eight tools are missing from the table entirely.
- `agent-docs/jusprin/architecture.md:137` — "which one tool each mode offers", plus its tap/undo wording.
